source_basis: OS Open Linked Identifiers documentation and technical specification

operations.detail: The evidence uses Ofcom official broadband checker.
The checker accepts a postcode or device location.
The checker reports broadband services predicted to be present at the selected location.
Displayed fixed broadband speeds are predictions supplied by network operators.
The checker displays the fastest estimated download and upload speeds.
Actual property availability or received speed may differ from the checker prediction.
Predicted speeds remain subject to service availability.
Standard broadband is classified below 30 Mbit/s download.
Superfast broadband is classified from 30 to 300 Mbit/s download.
Ultrafast broadband is classified above 300 Mbit/s download.
A green tick means packages are generally available in the area.
An amber triangle means packages are available to some but not all properties.
A red cross means packages in the category are not available.
Satellite broadband is shown separately from fixed line categories.
Fixed Wireless Access providers are presented separately.
The checker links to USO guidance where decent service may not be available.
The coverage checker cannot report maintenance or current network issues.
Users must consult their provider for current maintenance or incident information.
Ofcom provides developer access to fixed and mobile checker data through an API route.
The broadband checker presents predictions for a selected address or location.
A provider may not sell a package at the fastest predicted technical speed.
Checker values are not treated as measured customer speed tests.
A checker prediction is not treated as a contractual minimum-speed guarantee.
Checker display results do not replace validation of the official postcode archive.
No candidate is promoted from checker narrative or category semantics alone.
The mobile checker compares EE, Vodafone, O2 and Three.
Other mobile brands use one of the four host networks rather than appearing as independent radio networks.
Ordnance Survey data are used to identify properties for the mobile checker.
Property-address data are updated in the checker three times a year.
Mobile coverage is based on predictions supplied by the mobile network operators.
Predictions are generated by models simulating signal travel and obstruction.
Coverage predictions are processed into a 50 metre by 50 metre UK grid.
Ofcom performs real-world sample testing with dedicated measurement hardware.
Very local conditions can cause actual experience to differ from predictions.
Ofcom aims to refresh coverage about every three months or with Connected Nations.
Coverage predictions use average signal strength across an area.
Trees, buildings and hills can alter local signal experience.
Seasonal foliage can contribute to local variation.
Ofcom combines operator predictions under one independent standard.
The current checker excludes 2G and 3G as those networks are being switched off.
N/A or -1 is used where required prediction data are unavailable.
Coverage predictions and performance measurements use different methodologies.
Performance scores use crowdsourced smartphone measurements.
Crowdsourced measurements are handled by Opensignal and licensed to Ofcom.
Performance measurements are collected daily under normal use.
The measurement set includes indoor and outdoor usage.
Performance measurements are grouped to postal districts.
Performance is displayed as the percentage of samples meeting user-experience criteria.
Performance percentages use a rolling 12-month data window.
Scores are published only where measurements pass a statistical confidence threshold.
